{"run_id":"7d849360-6740-4cc6-bf14-63db7fb2d694","checkpoint":3,"role":"Writer","text":"A scheduled request arrives every two minutes. Does it need to reach the database every time?

In AI Journey Studio, the documented change was to validate signed integration requests, then return before database access if the request fell outside the configured source-intake and publishing windows.

The useful distinction: receiving a request and accessing the database became separate steps.

The repository’s build note, dated 25 October 2026, describes the project as an app for the owner’s AI learning journey, intended to help draft LinkedIn posts with separate owner approval before publication. Its previous setup included database reads from integration requests arriving every two minutes.

The change put a time-window check ahead of database access. Source intake used hourly windows; publication handling used exact configured windows.

That is a specific boundary—not a claim that the system checked whether an actual queued job was due. The condition was the configured work window.

What did the observations establish?

Neon provider checks on 25 October reported the production endpoint as suspended at three observed times. A separate Upstash metadata observation recorded a scheduled integration wake as successful.

Those findings have a limit: they do not establish that the scheduled request made no SQL queries, or that the database stayed asleep continuously. They also do not establish monthly compute savings or guaranteed use within the Free allowance.

So the practical method here is worth separating from the unmeasured outcome: check whether the request is inside its permitted work window before letting it access the database.

For a similar build, a useful instruction to give an agent could be:

“Inspect the scheduled-request path. Show where validation happens and where database access begins. The documented change put a boundary before database access: validate the signed request, then return early if it falls outside the configured source-intake and publishing windows.

Source intake used hourly windows. Publication handling used exact configured windows.

The condition matters: this checked the configured work window—not whether an actual queued job was due.

That is not proof that the scheduled request ran without database queries, or that the database stayed asleep continuously. Monthly compute savings were not established either.

The useful method here is the placement of the check: before database access, rather than after it.
